tier_reason: The jiakai1000/httpparsers README (Jan 2016) has pasted `time ./a.out N nginx|puma` runs: http_parser (joyent/Node.js 2.6.0) 4.064-4.066s vs Puma http11_parser 3.215-3.217s at 3M, and 6.778-6.780s vs 5.359-5.361s at 5M, plus /proc/cpuinfo (Xeon E5-2407). The code is public (puma1.c, http11_parser1.c, http_parser.c) and the Makefile says `gcc ... -O2`, but no GCC version is given and the recorded runs used ./a.out rather than the Makefile's `-o test` binary, so the flags actually used are not certain; C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ~1.26x faster (derived from page data): Puma http11_parser 3.215s vs http_parser 4.065s for 3M parses; 5.359s vs 6.778s for 5M parses (wall-clock `time`, three or two runs each, all within 0.003s)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc -O2 per the repo Makefile (GCC version not stated; the README runs use ./a.out, not the Makefile's `-o test` output, so the flags for the recorded numbers are not certain)
corrections.caveats: The benchmark repo (jiakai1000/httpparsers, 2 stars, no license) was a one-off from 2016-01-13 and has had no commits since. It measures the 2016 Puma parser against joyent http_parser 2.6.0 (now superseded by llhttp) on one repeated 9-header GET, with wall-clock `time` and one strcpy per iteration in both loops. It gives the CPU model and a -O2 Makefile but no GCC version, and the recorded runs used ./a.out, not the Makefile binary. The results are indicative, not rigorous. The Puma parser (ext/puma_http11) is Ragel-generated C from Zed Shaw's Mongrel and ships inside the Ruby gem; it is copyable under Puma's BSD-3-Clause license.

notes: The numbers match the README exactly; the ~1.26x ratio is derived from them. The record's caveat 'unmaintained since May 2025' was wrong: the benchmark repo's last commit is 2016-01-13. Puma metadata checks out (BSD-3-Clause, 7,917 stars, last commit 2026-09-16, not a fork, not archived).

tier_reason: The README Benchmarks table (measured 2026-08-07) lists sorug / ada-url / servo url at 28.3/31.9/97 ns, 56.0/140/216 ns, 196/277/248 ns and 31.1/95.0/129 ns, matching the claim. The Criterion code is public (benches/url_benchmark.rs, `cargo bench --bench url_benchmark`) and Cargo.toml [profile.bench] sets opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1. There is no CPU model (only 'Linux') and no rustc version, so it is first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: vs servo/url (derived from page data): ~3.4x on Fast Path ASCII (28.3 ns vs 97 ns), ~3.9x on Complex Query/Fragment (56.0 ns vs 216 ns), ~1.27x on IDNA/Punycode (196 ns vs 248 ns), ~4.1x on File Edge Case (31.1 ns vs 129 ns). The same table has sorug ahead of ada-url on all four workloads (28.3 vs 31.9, 56.0 vs 140, 196 vs 277, 31.1 vs 95.0 ns).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Cargo [profile.bench]: opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1 (Criterion 0.5); rustc version not stated (edition 2024, MSRV 1.85)
corrections.caveats: Entirely first-party and unreplicated. The README says 'Numbers are indicative. Absolute values vary by CPU; relative ordering is what we track', and it gives no CPU model or rustc version, only 'Linux'. The numbers were measured on 2026-08-07 during the 0.5/0.6 prep, and the current release is 0.6.2. sorug's parse borrows canonical ASCII input (Backing::Borrowed, copy-on-write), whereas url::Url::parse always builds an owned String, so part of the gap is an allocation the API design avoids. ada-url is measured through the ada-url 4 Rust FFI crate, not native C++ ada. The repo is young (created 2026-07-31) with 1 star, and the author has paused performance work until 1.0.

notes: The numbers match the README exactly; the ratios are derived. The record's caveat called the repo 'days-old', but it was created 2026-07-31, about 8 weeks before today. Metadata checks out: dual MIT OR Apache-2.0 per Cargo.toml and both LICENSE files (GitHub detects Apache-2.0), last commit 2026-09-21, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D. The record had no numbers page, but the maintainer's merged PR #40 (2018-06-22) has `cargo bench` results for httparse vs picohttpparser. The bench code is public (benches/parse.rs at v1.3.0, pico via the pico-sys crate) and the rustc version (1.27) and RUSTFLAGS are stated, but no CPU model is given (only 'my CPU has SSE4.2'). That is first-party C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: PR #40 (maintainer, rustc 1.27; pico built via pico-sys without SSE4.2): with -C target_cpu=native, httparse 405 ns vs pico 492 ns on the full browser request, ~1.21x (derived from page data), and 62 vs 72 ns on the short request, ~1.16x (derived). With runtime SIMD detection: 451 vs 492 ns, ~1.09x (derived), and 70 vs 72 ns. With SIMD off, httparse is slower on the full request (529 vs 492 ns) and faster only on the short one (66 vs 72 ns). The maintainer's summary: 'Without SIMD, httparse is oh-so-slightly faster than Pico when the requests are tiny, but a bit slower on a more realist request from a browser.' The record's 'faster than picohttpparser, when SIMD is not available' (lib.rs doc v1.2.3-v1.2.5, removed in v1.3.0) never came with numbers, and PR #40 contradicts it for realistic requests.
corrections.workload: Rust nightly #[bench] with [profile.bench] lto=true (benches/parse.rs at v1.3.0). It parses one fixed ~700-byte, 10-header browser GET request (the 'hello-kitty-darth-vader' request) and one 3-line short request. picohttpparser is called over FFI through the pico-sys 0.0.1 crate.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.27 (nightly bench harness), [profile.bench] lto=true; runs with SIMD off, with runtime SSE4.2/AVX2 detection, and with -C target_cpu=native. pico-sys compiles picohttpparser.c through the gcc crate with no -msse4.2, so pico runs its non-SSE4.2 path.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 714 GitHub stars; ~742M crates.io downloads (~169M recent); the de facto HTTP/1.x parser for Rust (hyper, actix-web and most of the Rust HTTP ecosystem)
corrections.caveats: The only measured wins over picohttpparser pit httparse's SIMD paths against pico built without SSE4.2 (pico-sys uses default cc flags). Issue #85 (2021, still open) says this is not apples to apples, and the maintainer replied 'good point'. With pico built with -msse4 plus cross-language LTO, a third-party user reported pico at ~2900 MB/s vs httparse at 1751 MB/s (text in issue #85, full tables only as images). With both parsers' SIMD off, the maintainer's own PR #40 shows httparse slower on the realistic request (529 vs 492 ns) and ahead only on a tiny request (66 vs 72 ns). The 2018 contributor PR #38 shows it slower on both without SIMD (468 vs 405 ns, 54 vs 53 ns). No CPU model is given anywhere, and the numbers date from 2018. PR #112 (2022) removed the pico targets from benches, so current code no longer compares against picohttpparser. The out-of-the-box edge is real but fragile: httparse's runtime SIMD detection beats a generically built pico by ~1.09x on the full request.

notes: The record's claim sentence is real (lib.rs doc in 1.2.3-1.2.5; v1.0-1.2.0 said '1.6 times slower than pico'), but the project's own later numbers contradict it for realistic requests. I kept the entry at C on PR #40, whose SIMD httparse beats non-SSE4.2 pico by 1.09-1.21x, and flagged the unfair-baseline issue (#85). If the orchestrator wants fair-baseline evidence only, this is a reject candidate ('not-faster'), because the only fair-build report has pico ~1.66x faster. Metadata checks out: MIT OR Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-06-30, not a fork, not archived.
